title: Take Comfort That Time Brings Bereavements
intro: Ibn al-Rumi’s diwan addresses this consolation to Ubayd Allah ibn Abd Allah on his mother’s death. It begins with things a bereaved person has long known and asks why knowing them does so little to prevent the shock. The argument changes when the poet recalls the mother at prayer, asking that her child might outlive her. He ends by wishing the son a full life before their reunion.

translation: Take comfort that time brings bereavements
and everything once joined must come apart.
1.sharh: The opening names neither mourner nor mother. It starts with a word for something brought together and makes the listener hear its opposite at the rhyme.

translation: God bless you, how often have you seen or heard of
a clan whose companions were never torn apart?
2.sharh: The mourner can consult both memory and report for a company that has stayed together. A brief blessing softens the challenge to find one.

translation: What are people but the offspring of a drop,
crumbling in the end to dust, to utter dust?
3.sharh: Two bodily states frame a whole lifetime. Repeating “dust” makes the listener dwell on the disintegration that the compressed account might otherwise hurry past.

translation: Lowly drops of fluid find their end
in the crumbled remains of hollow bones.
4.sharh: The extremes are fluid and brittle bone. The living, solid body that once seemed permanent is the missing middle of the picture.

translation: I see time as a mount forever carrying a rider.
If it slips, who is safe from a fall?
5.sharh: One rider can give place to another while the mount keeps moving. The surest seat offers little security when the animal itself slips.

translation: A strange thing, the harder we ride it,
the farther we get from what we seek.
6.sharh: The mount carries us through our finite span of time. Riding harder can use up the very interval in which our purposes might be achieved.

translation: Stranger still, our eagerness grows as our years go by,
as if we were still children of ten.
7.sharh: The child imagines a long future on which to draw. An older person goes on spending that imaginary credit even as the years available grow fewer.

translation: We leave our hopes behind us as though
we were moving towards them, away from the deep waters.
8.sharh: Hopes often look like landmarks ahead of us. In this backward glance they are the things left unfulfilled along the road, while deeper and more dangerous waters lie ahead.

translation: We were beguiled and warned by an age that wearied us
with lures and warnings, with “take this” and “give it here”.
9.sharh: The two imperatives make time sound like someone passing a gift across a counter and calling it back. Each experience contains a warning about the next.

translation: Whenever it spits out mouthfuls of honey, they are followed
by far-reaching arrows with the sharpest points.
10.sharh: The honey arrives in little mouthfuls. Time’s next gift can strike at a distance, and its sharpness makes the earlier sweetness feel dangerously persuasive.

translation: My prince, your judgement rises like a star,
and travellers steer by it through the dark.
11.sharh: Only now does he address the prince. A verb for a star rising makes practical sense of the compliment, since a traveller can actually steer by it.

translation: The wind of calamity blows fierce when it rises,
and you stand like the flank of a mountain of ridges.
12.sharh: Wind gives the calamity a direction and force. The many ridges behind the mountain flank give the prince something solid against which to hold his ground.

translation: Hold fast to reverence for God and to patience. Patience
is a refuge, and time has its assaults.
13.sharh: Praise has described a steady man. The advice now supplies somewhere for him to stand while time is still capable of striking again.

translation: The wise man of a people is no man
who sees his afflictions as acts of vengeance.
14.sharh: Suffering and interpreting suffering are separate acts. Bereavement need carry no accusation against the person left alive.

translation: You have been bereaved. May no such grief return,
a loss such as kings suffer in losing queens.
15.sharh: The sentence admitting what happened is interrupted by a wish that it never happen again. Kings losing queens give a scale for how great this woman was to the mourner.

translation: You have been struck, as everyone is struck by a blow
that breaks open an old injury from former blows.
16.sharh: The verb belongs to a fracture reopened after healing. The latest bereavement hurts in places where a person had already sustained and survived a loss.

translation: Do not give way under it, though a loss like this
could make even a quiet heart recoil.
17.sharh: The second half allows the immediate recoil of a steady man. The call for endurance takes the force of the shock into account.

translation: Why should a soul recoil when trouble comes
after so long knowing what was bound to come?
18.sharh: For a long time the mind has known the fact of mortality. It is the arrival of a particular instance at one’s own door that turns knowledge into a start of fear.

translation: Can it be certain of what is decreed before it happens,
then start like someone green and heedless?
19.sharh: The grammar holds knowledge and alarm together in one subject. In its bodily response the experienced soul can still behave like a novice.

translation: It has been familiarised until it is time it grew familiar
with the blows it has seen time deal.
20.sharh: The same Arabic root appears first in the passive and then as the soul’s own familiarity. Long exposure to grief and feeling at home with it turn out to be different achievements.

translation: Why does it recoil with all the recoil of the inexperienced,
after receiving so many warnings by example?
21.sharh: Other people’s suffering has furnished examples enough. The doubled word for recoil catches how stubbornly the soul’s first movement survives all those lessons.

translation: Whoever reckons with what is decreed learns certainty. To him
what has pitched camp and what is awaited stand alike.
22.sharh: Calamities already present have made their camels kneel at the destination. Those still on the road differ in their date of arrival, a distinction forethought can narrow.

translation: In this low world what can anyone await
except losing a loved one or meeting death himself?
23.sharh: For two people who love each other there are two positions at the end, to go first or to be left. In Arabic the words for this world and for its lowliness nearly coincide.

translation: Have you not seen calamity’s raids press on,
now attacking at dawn, now holding their ground?
24.sharh: Trouble is pictured as raiders who can surprise a camp early or remain in place. The people they visit have no say in their timetable.

translation: They come at evening and morning, never flagging,
to living things by turns and to the lifeless.
25.sharh: Evening and morning give the raids a routine. Their reach extends past human lives to objects that wear away without ever having lived.

translation: Time’s movements in every blink of the eye
are never too occupied for these movements of destruction.
26.sharh: Each blink looks too short to matter. Reusing the word “movements” brings that almost imperceptible passage and time’s work of destruction into one frame.

translation: It will give the children of this world their cups of death
until they sleep a sleep beyond ordinary slumber.
27.sharh: Time now passes cups round a company. The sleep that follows the drink borrows a familiar nightly experience and takes away its ordinary morning ending.

translation: The days’ treachery is surely a kind of fidelity.
Do they ever do anything but keep their promises?
28.sharh: The days have given ample notice of their habit of betrayal. Measured by how closely conduct matches a warning, they are remarkably true to their word.

translation: They promise betrayal and never break that promise.
Consider such good faith in a practised traitor.
29.sharh: The content of the promise resolves the verbal puzzle. The last phrase turns the abstract days into a recognisable character with a record of repeated betrayals.

translation: Take heart at the deaths of the noble men of Mus'ab’s house.
You can find consolation in them, or examples to follow.
30.sharh: The prince can turn to his own family history in two ways. Its dead keep him company in loss, and the way they once bore loss gives him an example.

translation: They took comfort when every kind of trouble visited them.
In dying they in turn consoled every grieving heart.
31.sharh: The same consolation travels through successive generations. People who once needed it can go on giving it by the very fact that they too have died.

translation: Among the customs God has established for humankind,
as thoughts range about seeking lessons,
32.sharh: The sentence opens a place for a particular pattern and leaves it empty at the rhyme. The listener must wait through the pause for the human observation that fills it.

translation: is for people’s roots to go before their branches.
Neither of the two has lasting tenure.
33.sharh: The mother is a root and the surviving child a branch. The ordinary order of their loss offers an explanation for the present without promising the survivor permanence.

translation: So something new survives what has worn away. All of them
will wear out through the summers and the winters.
34.sharh: Generations take the places of worn things while they themselves are still new. The alternation of seasons gives that wearing-out an everyday measure.

translation: If a branch goes before its root,
that counts among the unexpected turns and sudden events.
35.sharh: He allows for the bereavement in which a parent must bury a child. “Unexpected” describes how people experience that reversal of the ordinary order.

translation: These too are decrees of God, exalted be his praise.
God’s decrees admit of no slips.
36.sharh: A surprising event might be called a slip in ordinary speech. He draws a theological boundary around that usage when it touches the ordering of deaths.

translation: So we may know that none dies simply of old age,
nor does anyone live by virtue of fresh growth.
37.sharh: New growth is something on which we naturally count for a future. An early death exposes how little assurance youth or age can offer about who will outlive whom.

translation: The one you have sent ahead went in her due order.
Let the streaming tears and heavy sighs go.
38.sharh: The survivor has quite literally seen her on her way. Tears and breath bring the large argument about generations back to the physical labour of grieving.

translation: Do not resent the truth that accords with right guidance
and with the wish of the one for whom you grieve.
39.sharh: The argument gains a new witness. The very person on whose account he grieves once wanted this order of things for him.

translation: You lost the woman who wished you to live on after her
and kept her prayers for you alive through the night.
40.sharh: What was a proposition about parents becomes the picture of a woman awake at night. Her son’s continuing life gives those otherwise private prayers a visible answer.

translation: She wished that her own bier should come first.
Some of the soul’s wishes do come to meet it.
41.sharh: The bier makes the mother’s prayer painfully concrete. Of the two possible funerals it was her own that she wanted her child to survive.

translation: Do not begrudge her the thing she wanted.
To hate what she wished for would be a strange return.
42.sharh: He asks the mourner to look at the same event from the other side of their relationship. The son’s loss and the granting of her wish can occupy the same day.

translation: Did you not see time’s loss before it happened,
face to face, when you thought in solitude?
43.sharh: “Face to face” ordinarily requires another presence. Solitary thought has given a future loss enough shape to confront the prince before its arrival.

translation: You did meet it, though it was absent,
in your mind. Thought makes raids of its own.
44.sharh: The raids that belonged to calamity now belong to thought as well. The mind can travel out to meet trouble instead of always waiting to be attacked at home.

translation: Why then be like a man struck in his place of safety
by arrows that had shunned him, arrows unforeseen?
45.sharh: The victim had trusted his shelter and counted himself out of the arrows’ reach. Al-Raghib’s version says the arrows “came to him”. Both versions end with the victim’s failure to anticipate them.

translation: Rein in your heart. Bereavements are blows
that hit their mark, though they were reckoned with beforehand.
46.sharh: A verbal echo makes calamities into things that have “hit” someone. Being prepared cannot deflect the blow, but it gives the mourner something to do with the heart that receives it.

translation: If you say, “An evil came on me all at once”,
what heart that entertains such thoughts was caught wholly unawares?
47.sharh: The mourner finally gets a word in. The reply turns on a real distinction between never having imagined a loss and never having known its appointed hour.

translation: No soul is taken unawares by affliction after seeing
one warning from the days upon another.
48.sharh: The evidence has accumulated outside the mourner’s mind as well. Repeating “warning” gives each loss he has witnessed its place in that slow education.

translation: If things happen suddenly whose like has happened
long ago, do not count them as surprises.
49.sharh: One word for suddenness returns as both event and judgement. He allows the moment its shock while asking whether its kind can really be called unprecedented.

translation: You faltered, though men speak of your resolve.
Even the wide awake must sometimes sleep.
50.sharh: The comparison gives the prince a way to admit a lapse without surrendering his entire reputation. Even a vigilant person’s day contains sleep.

translation: Let wakefulness follow on that sleep, and go wisely.
Even sleepers are bound to have awakenings.
51.sharh: Turning the previous observation round also reverses its emotional direction. The lapse that explained his grief can now be the beginning of recovery.

translation: Someone who resists the Devil as you do will never answer
his charms or follow his footsteps.
52.sharh: Temptation first tries to draw him by sound, then leaves a track for his feet. His earlier resistance is appealed to as a resource available in the present.

translation: Among the things that ease your grief are her good deeds.
You yourself are one of them, man of good deeds.
53.sharh: “Of them” can count the son among her good works just as descent makes him “of her”. The mourner is himself evidence that part of her work survives.

translation: God’s reward for bearing the loss of a woman like her
is to meet her in the highest ranks.
54.sharh: The poem began with every union coming apart. Its promise now holds mother and son together inside a single Arabic word for meeting.

translation: That will be when you have fulfilled every longing
for honour and enjoyed all life’s pleasures.
55.sharh: The promised reunion carries no wish for the son’s early death. Letting him finish his own life also allows his mother’s prayer to be fulfilled to the end.

translation: She went after being granted a stretch of time on earth
to give its people blessings in abundance.
56.sharh: Her years are measured by what reached other people through them. The sense of abundance prepares the next image of branches laden with fruit.

translation: If Tuba has gone back to her sister trees,
she has been provisioned with good fruit.
57.sharh: The paradisal tree gives the mother a home to go back to. Good deeds can now be pictured both as the fruit she bore and as provisions for the way.

translation: By your life, she was never led in procession to a pit.
She was led like a bride to the chambers on high.
58.sharh: The procession takes its verb from the escorting of a bride. Its destination changes with the mourner’s point of view, from the depth he can see to the height he hopes for.

translation: Were it not for you, we would ask who could fill her place,
who could choose reverence for God over doubtful things.
59.sharh: The son answers a question that would otherwise remain open. What he can continue of her life is a habit of choosing cautiously when right conduct is in doubt.

translation: May life-giving rain water her along with the tears shed for her,
at evening departures and at morning’s first stirrings.
60.sharh: Tears once appeared as a flood the mourner should check. Here they can fall alongside nourishing rain, giving sorrow a place in the final blessing.

translation: May she be blessed whenever the sun rises
or sets, by the One to whom prayers belong.
61.sharh: The subject of the blessing is held until the last words. The alternation of days that formerly wore things away now measures how often the prayer can be renewed.

1.1.5.head: فَجعَة
1.1.5.meaning: A sudden bereavement or grievous loss.

2.2.1.head: قَرينَة
2.2.1.meaning: A companion or partner bound to another in life.

2.2.4.head: مُختَلَج
2.2.4.meaning: Snatched away or torn from its fellows.

3.1.6.head: سُلالَة
3.1.6.meaning: An extracted essence, here the fluid from which human life begins.

3.2.2.head: رُفات
3.2.2.meaning: Remains that have crumbled into fragments or dust.

4.2.5.head: نَخِر
4.2.5.meaning: Hollowed or eaten away by decay.

5.1.3.head: ظَهر
5.1.3.meaning: A riding beast, named for the back that carries a rider.

6.2.4.head: طَلِبَة
6.2.4.meaning: An object of pursuit or something one wishes to obtain.

7.2.4-5.head: بَنو العَشَرات
7.2.4-5.meaning: “Children of the tens”, youngsters who still have most of their years ahead.

8.2.5.head: غَمرَة
8.2.5.meaning: Deep water, hence an overwhelming ordeal.

9.2.3-4.head: هاكَ وَهاتِ
9.2.3-4.meaning: “Take this and give it here”, the two motions of giving and reclaiming.

11.1.4.head: نَجَمَ
11.1.4.meaning: Rose into view like a star.

11.2.3.head: سارٍ
11.2.3.meaning: A traveller who goes by night.

14.2.4.head: نَقِمَة
14.2.4.meaning: A punitive blow or act of vengeance.

16.2.1.head: هاضَ
16.2.1.meaning: Broke a healing bone again, here reopened an old grief.

17.2.1.head: زَعيم
17.2.1.meaning: A guarantor, here something sure to cause an effect.

17.2.3.head: الجَأش
17.2.3.meaning: The heart or spirit as the seat of composure.

19.2.3.head: الغِرّ
19.2.3.meaning: A novice, someone easily taken in.

21.2.5.head: مَثُلَة
21.2.5.meaning: A suffering or punishment that serves as an example to others.

22.2.2.head: مُنيخ
22.2.2.meaning: Halted at a destination like a kneeling camel.

24.2.2.head: مُغاداة
24.2.2.meaning: Coming upon someone at dawn, here as a raider.

26.1.6.head: طَرفَة
26.1.6.meaning: The time of a single blink.

29.1.4.head: أَخلَفَ
29.1.4.meaning: Failed to keep a promise, here the very promise of betrayal.

30.1.3.head: الصّيد
30.1.3.meaning: Noble, proud men, literally men who hold their heads high.

30.1.5-6.head: آل مُصعَب
30.1.5-6.meaning: The house of Mus'ab, the family from which the Tahirids traced descent.

30.2.2.head: أُسى
30.2.2.meaning: Examples in whom a mourner finds comfort.

32.2.4.head: مُعتَبِر
32.2.4.meaning: Taking a lesson from what one has seen.

37.2.4.head: اِقتِبال
37.2.4.meaning: The onset of something, here the beginnings of growth.

41.1.5.head: سَرير
41.1.5.meaning: The bier on which the dead are carried.

41.2.4.head: مُواتٍ
41.2.4.meaning: Coming to meet a wish, fulfilled.

42.2.5.head: نُكرَة
42.2.5.meaning: Something objectionable or hard to countenance.

44.2.5.head: غَزوَة
44.2.5.meaning: A raid or expedition, here the mind’s reach beyond the present.

45.2.2.head: أَبى
45.2.2.meaning: Refused or shunned. The arrows seem to have passed him by until this blow. Al-Raghib quotes the clearer reading “came to him”.

50.2.3.head: الأَيقاظ
50.2.3.meaning: Those who are awake or watchful.

53.1.3.meaning: Grief over someone or something lost.

54.2.1.head: لِقاء
54.2.1.meaning: A meeting, with the Arabic suffixes joining the son and his mother in one word.

57.1.3.meaning: Tuba, a tree of Paradise in Islamic tradition.

58.1.3.head: زُفَّ
58.1.3.meaning: Was escorted in procession, especially of a bride.

58.2.4.head: الغُرُفات
58.2.4.meaning: Lofty chambers, here the dwellings of Paradise.

59.2.5.head: الشُّبُهات
59.2.5.meaning: Doubtful matters whose moral status is unclear.

60.2.1.meaning: Rain that gives life to the land.

60.2.4-5.head: الرَّوحات وَالغَدَوات
60.2.4-5.meaning: Evening and morning rounds or departures.

61.1.4.meaning: Rose or sent out its first ray.

61.1.5.head: شارِق
61.1.5.meaning: The rising sun or its first light.

47.1.4.head: أَلَمَّ
47.1.4.meaning: Befell. The feminine verb suggests a calamity understood from the preceding verse. The unvowelled letters also allow “I felt pain”. Al-Raghib’s excerpt has “came upon me”.
